5.html:
Note · Who counts as a zakenah?

זְקֵנָה כָּל שֶׁעָבְרוּ עָלֶיהָ תִּשְׁעִים יוֹם סָמוּךְ לְזִקְנָתָהּ. וְאֵי זוֹ הִיא זְקֵנָה כָּל שֶׁקּוֹרְאִין לָהּ זְקֵנָה וְאֵינָהּ מַקְפֶּדֶת.

“The term ‘elderly woman’ refers to a woman who did not menstruate for 90 days near her old age. When is she considered elderly? When she is called an old woman [by others] and she does not protest.”

The definition here is not a fixed age. It is two conditions together: ninety days without menstruation near old age, and social recognition — people call her zakenah, and she does not object. The legal consequence, in this chapter, is narrow: like a pregnant or nursing woman, her stain is treated like a sighting, and it does not defile retroactively (halachot 4–5).

Do not collapse this into the other zaken definitions. Kiddushin 32b's zaken is zeh shekanah chochmah, one who has acquired wisdom; Bava Metzia 30's zaken ve'eino lefi kvodo is about dignity in returning a lost object. This one is a niddah category, defined by body and by what people call her.

Source: Daily Reader, 28 October 2026 — Rambam Yomi, Issurei Biah 9:5.

37.html:
Note · The seven cleaning agents, in order

וְאֵלּוּ הֵן הַשִּׁבְעָה סַמָּנִים עַל סִדְרָן. רֹק תָּפֵל. וּלְעִיסַת גְּרִיסִין שֶׁל פּוֹל. וּמֵי רַגְלַיִם שֶׁהֶחֱמִיצוּ. וּבֹרִית. וְנֶתֶר. וְקִימוֹנְיָא. וְאַשְׁלָג.

In order, from halachah 37:

  • רֹק תָּפֵל — saliva of one who has not eaten (defined in halachah 38: from the night, slept the second half of the night, before eating, and without much speech in the first three hours of the day)
  • לְעִיסַת גְּרִיסִין שֶׁל פּוֹל — chewed bean gruel, chewed until well mixed with saliva
  • מֵי רַגְלַיִם שֶׁהֶחֱמִיצוּ — urine that has soured, three days old or more
  • בֹּרִית — lye / soapwort
  • נֶתֶר — natron
  • קִימוֹנְיָא — Cimolian earth, not cumin (see below)
  • אַשְׁלָג — potash, not modern bleach (see below)

Procedure matters as much as the list: rub three times with each agent, passing back and forth with each rub. Out of order, or all at once, counts for nothing. If the later ones were used first, they count as the first ones in order, and the rest are then applied after them until all seven have run in order.

Why run them at all? Halachah 36: a stain on a garment with nothing to attribute it to does not defile until it is proven to be blood. If it is doubtful whether it is blood or red dye, run the seven agents in order. If it fades or weakens, it is a bloodstain; if it stands as it was, it is dye.

On the two hard words. קִימוֹנְיָא is Cimolian earth — Greek κιμωλία, from the island of Kimolos, a clay used in the ancient world for bleaching and washing clothes. Cumin is a different word, כמון. The identification is disputed: Maimonides himself identified kimonia as a plant-derived alkaline substance, while other commentators identify it with Cimolian earth. אַשְׁלָג is potash, an alkaline salt — the ancestor of bleaching agents, not the modern product.

And not economica. Modern Israeli bleach is called אקונומיקה, but not from קִימוֹנְיָא. It is a 1940s Jerusalem brand name, trademarked in 1945, from English “economic” — thrifty household management — which then became the generic word for bleach. The resemblance is a coincidence; the two bleaching traditions are two thousand years apart.

Source: Daily Reader, 28 October 2026 — Rambam Yomi, Issurei Biah 9:36–38.

24.html:
Note · Cruelty costs a people its place

וְלָמָּה גָּזַר עֲלֵיהֶם הוּא וּבֵית דִּינוֹ לְפִי שֶׁרָאָה עַזּוּת וְאַכְזָרִיּוּת שֶׁהָיְתָה בָּהֶם בְּעֵת שֶׁבִּקְּשׁוּ שִׁבְעַת בְּנֵי שָׁאוּל בְּחִיר ה' לִתְלוֹתָם וַהֲרָגוּם וְלֹא רִחֲמוּ עֲלֵיהֶם:

“Why did David and his court pass this decree against them? Because he saw that they were characterized by brazenness and cruelty. For they asked to kill and hang the seven sons of Saul, God's chosen one, and they did not have mercy upon them.”

The backstory is II Samuel 21: three years of famine, and David learns through prophetic vision that the cause is Saul's oppression of the Gibeonites. He asks what will appease them. They demand seven of Saul's descendants, hang them, and leave the corpses on the gallows.

The Rambam's point is that the decree is diagnostic, not only punitive. Brazenness and cruelty travel together — עַזּוּת וְאַכְזָרִיּוּת — the Gibeonites would not be appeased and would not show mercy, and that failure is what marks them as outside Israel, permanently: they may never marry into the Jewish people.

The counter-mark is Yevamot 79a: “There are three distinguishing marks of this nation: the merciful, the shamefaced, and the performers of kindness” — הָרַחְמָנִים, וְהַבַּיְישָׁנִין, וְגוֹמְלֵי חֲסָדִים. Mercy is not decoration here; it is the membership test.

The arc closes in Issurei Biah 19:17: “whenever a person is characterized by insolence and cruelty, hating people and not showing kindness to them, we seriously suspect that he is a Gibeonite. For the distinguishing signs of the holy nation of Israel is that they are meek, merciful, and kind.” And the sting in 19:17: the Jews had shown the Gibeonites kindness and let them live (Joshua 9) — the cruelty was repaid kindness answered with cruelty.

So cruelty, for the Rambam, is not a mood or a single act. It is a character that refuses appeasement and refuses mercy — and it disqualifies.

Sources: II Samuel 21; Yevamot 79a; Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:17.
